<reason>CON (Side A) won by progressively narrowing PRO's case using PRO's own concessions: tests must be secret and rotating (undercutting public comparability), redacted details travel confidentially to regulators (making publication informationally thin), and a developer can publish adverse findings and ship the next day (so the motion blocks no harm). CON's pressure questions extracted real admissions and its A1/A2 answers were direct, notably catching that PRO's preventive mechanism was the reputational pressure PRO's own opening dismissed. PRO argued competently and honestly—its externality framing, "evidence before exposure" reframe, and timing distinction in the closing were real answers—but it stayed defensive, never squarely dislodged the certificate-effect and incumbency-cost points, and left the public-facing value of the mandated report looking like a category-level statement plus a completion stamp. CON made the decision easier; PRO kept a live but weakened route.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.1–A4.2: after PRO conceded that developers may deploy the day after publishing adverse results and that the preventive force is commercial/reputational cost, CON pointed out this is exactly the mechanism PRO's opening [B1.2] rejected as arriving too late, collapsing PRO's prevention story into the comparison CON wanted.</best_rebuttal>
